docs.text: The Kokeb Labs handbook ¶ How every Kokeb Labs repository is designed, written, tested, documented and released, for people and for coding agents alike. Every rule here has an ID, a level and a stated way of being verified. Most are checked by CI on every pull request; the rest are checked in review against the pull-request checklist, or are guidance, and say so. A rule nobody can verify is not written as a rule. Where to start ¶ You want to Read Understand how rules, IDs, levels and checks work How rules work Know what your repository has to meet Assurance levels , then the rules for your kind Set a rule aside for a good reason Deviations and waivers See how much is verified by CI today Coverage Use a Kokeb component in a regulated product Evidence for regulated products and IEC 62304 Know which coding standards we follow Coding standards Read why a decision was made Decision records Read the design of each layer Standards What it covers ¶ C and C++20 code, CMake, tests, Markdown and Doxygen documentation, repository layout, Git and releases, CI and supply chain, and coding agents, for drivers, libraries, board HALs, firmware, tooling and documentation repositories. Who it is for ¶ Contributors and maintainers of Kokeb Labs repositories, coding agents working in them (each repository's AGENTS.md carries the rules for its kind), and teams that build products on Kokeb components and need to know what was verified and how. Product families under the Kokeb Labs umbrella extend this handbook with their own supplement, in the same format and checked by the same tools; HardFOC's is hardfoc/hf-development-handbook . A supplement adds rules; it never relaxes one of these.

docs.text: Assurance levels ¶ Not every repository needs the same rigour. A script that renders a diagram and a motor-current driver inside a medical pump are both Kokeb code, but only one of them can hurt someone. Each repository declares one of three levels, and each level includes everything below it. All levels keep the same rules; higher levels switch on more of them and ask for more evidence. Level For Adds standard Every repository: tools, examples, documentation Format, lint, static analysis, host tests, strict docs build, DCO, the CI gate high Code others build products on: drivers, kb-core, board HALs Sanitizers; a coverage floor (85% lines, 75% branches); builds for every supported target; warning-free Doxygen on the public API; a deviation record for every suppressed finding; register layouts asserted safety Components meant to be qualified inside a safety-classified product, such as the software of an IEC 62304 class C medical device Requirements traced to code and tests; every reachable branch covered, each gap justified; the coding-standard compliance matrix with a commercial MISRA checker run; an anomaly list; a signed evidence package per release Choosing a level ¶ A repository starts at standard and moves up when something depends on it. Drivers and kb-core are high from their first release. safety is chosen per component when a product team intends to qualify it, and needs the maintainer's approval in a decision record, because it commits the project to keeping the evidence current for every release. What a level is not ¶ A level is not a certification. A Kokeb component at safety level is not "IEC 62304 compliant": compliance is a property of a manufacturer's process and product, not of a library. What the level guarantees is that the evidence a manufacturer's process asks for exists, is complete, and was produced by the checks named here. See IEC 62304 for how that maps onto the standard.

docs.text: Coding standards ¶ Kokeb Labs code follows named, published coding standards, so that a reviewer, an auditor or a customer can check our claims against a reference they already know. Standard Used for How we follow it MISRA C++:2023 (with TC1:2026) C++ code Reference standard. A compliance matrix classifies every guideline (below). MISRA C:2025 C code Reference standard; its compliance matrix follows the same format (not written yet). SEI CERT C++ and CERT C Security baseline Every rule an open tool can decide is checked by clang-tidy ( cert-* ) or cppcheck. C++ Core Guidelines Design and idiom Followed through the clang-tidy cppcoreguidelines-* checks and the Standards pages. NASA/JPL Power of Ten Embedded discipline Covered by rules on memory, loops and checking every result. What "follows MISRA" means here ¶ We use the approach MISRA itself defines in MISRA Compliance:2020 : Guideline enforcement plan. For every guideline of MISRA C++:2023, the compliance matrix ( compliance/misra-cpp-2023.yml ) records how it is verified (MISRA C:2025 gets compliance/misra-c-2025.yml in the same format): tool: a named clang-tidy or cppcheck check, or a compiler flag, that decides it; review: it is undecidable or no open tool decides it, so it is on the pull-request checklist; commercial checker: decided by the MISRA checker that the safety level adds; not applicable: the construct cannot occur in our code (for example, guidelines about exceptions, which we do not use), with the reason. Guideline re-categorisation plan. Where our profile is stricter than MISRA (an advisory guideline we treat as required), the matrix says so. We never make a guideline weaker than MISRA classifies it. Deviations. Every departure from a required guideline has a deviation record : project-wide ones in compliance/misra-cpp-2023-deviations.yml , single places in the repository's own docs/deviations.yml . Mandatory guidelines are never deviated. Compliance summary. Each release of a high or safety component states, per guideline, whether it is compliant, deviated or not applicable. It is generated from the matrix and the deviation records. The edition ¶ The matrix is written against MISRA C++:2023 with Technical Corrigendum 1 (TC1:2026) . The corrigendum adds no guidelines and is equivalent to MISRA C++:2023, but clarifies many of them, so tool reports can differ from the 2023 text. The licensed copy the matrix was written from is held privately by the maintainer; the matrix records its SHA-256 ( licensed_copy_sha256 ), so any entry can be traced to the exact edition it was checked against. When MISRA publishes a new corrigendum or edition, the matrix is reviewed against it in one pull request that changes the hash. MISRA C++:2023 targets C++17; our code is C++20 (ADR-0010). Deviation MD-CPP-001 records that, lists the C++20 features in use, and says how each guideline applies to C++20 constructs. Reading the matrix ¶ Each guideline has one entry: Field Meaning id The guideline number, Rule a.b.c or Dir a.b.c . kind rule (checkable from the code alone) or directive (needs design or requirements information). category MISRA's category: mandatory , required or advisory . decidable Whether an analyser can always answer "compliant?" ( yes / no ); n/a for directives. scope tu when one translation unit at a time is enough, system when the whole program is needed. summary Our own one-line paraphrase (at most 12 words); the standard's text is not reproduced. applies yes , or no with a reason (for example, the exception guidelines: we build with -fno-exceptions ). our_category The category we enforce: MISRA's or stricter, never weaker. A stricter one is our re-categorisation plan. verification How it is checked: each item names by (method) and how (the exact flag, check or review step). deviations The project-wide deviation records that cover part of the guideline, if any. note Anything a reader needs to apply the guideline to our code. The verification methods are: compiler : a GCC or Clang flag (with -Werror ) whose diagnostic decides the guideline; clang-tidy : a clang-tidy 20 check, with its options where they matter; cppcheck : a cppcheck message id (there is no free MISRA C++ addon; cppcheck's MISRA addon covers MISRA C only); handbook-check : one of the handbook's own implemented checks ( checks/source_checks.py for include guards and pragmas, ci-tools' handbook check for the forbidden patterns); review : the step a reviewer checks on the pull request, used where no free tool decides the guideline; commercial-checker : the MISRA checker the safety level adds, for every guideline no free tool decides; not-applicable : the construct cannot occur in our code, and why. A tool item marked partial: true finds some violations but cannot prove there are none (an undecidable guideline, or a check narrower than the guideline); such a guideline always also has a review step and the commercial checker. A tool is only listed for a guideline it actually checks. The clang-tidy checks the matrix names are split between two profiles (next section). checks/misra_matrix.py validates the matrix and the deviations on every pull request: every guideline present exactly once (179), valid categories, our_category never weaker, a verification for every applicable guideline, a reason for every guideline that does not apply, and no deviation of a mandatory guideline. It also keeps the counts below current. Counts ¶ MISRA C++:2023 with TC1:2026 has 179 guidelines : 4 directives and 175 rules. MISRA category Directives Rules Total Our category mandatory 0 5 5 5 required 2 122 124 131 advisory 2 48 50 43 all 4 175 179 179 How it is verified Guidelines Decided by an open tool (compiler, clang-tidy, cppcheck, handbook check) 48 of which by compiler 11 of which by clang-tidy 35 of which by handbook-check 2 Review and commercial checker, helped by a partial tool 79 Review and commercial checker only 45 Not applicable to our code 7 A guideline can be decided by more than one tool. Raised above MISRA's category: 7 (Dir 5.7.2, Rule 6.0.3, Rule 9.6.1, Rule 10.2.2, Rule 12.2.1, Rule 13.1.1, Rule 21.6.1). Project-wide deviations: 8 (MD-CPP-001 Rule 4.1.1, MD-CPP-002 Rule 16.6.1, MD-CPP-003 Rule 8.2.5, MD-CPP-004 Rule 8.2.6, MD-CPP-005 Rule 6.7.2, MD-CPP-006 Rule 19.0.2, MD-CPP-007 Rule 21.2.4, MD-CPP-008 Rule 21.6.1). clang-tidy profiles ¶ Most of the clang-tidy checks the matrix names are in the org's default configuration ( config/.clang-tidy ), which every repository at the standard and high levels uses. The rest are in the safety-level profile ( config/.clang-tidy-safety ): the default plus every check the matrix names that the default leaves off, with the stricter options those guidelines need. The profile is generated by python checks/misra_matrix.py gen from the default and the matrix, and CI fails if it is stale, so the two cannot drift. python checks/misra_matrix.py tidy prints both lists. Checks the matrix relies on that are on at every level, because they are cheap and fit the code: Check Guideline Note hicpp-signed-bitwise Rules 7.0.4, 7.0.5 IgnorePositiveIntegerLiterals : 1U << 3 passes; a uint8_t promoted to int before << , ~ or | does not, so cast to uint32_t first readability-uppercase-literal-suffix Rule 5.13.5 NewSuffixes: L;LL;UL;ULL ; 0xFFu and 1.0f stay accepted misc-no-recursion Rule 8.2.10 within one translation unit misc-static-assert Rule 22.3.1 misc-definitions-in-headers Rule 6.2.4 .ipp counts as a header misc-unconventional-assign-operator Rule 15.0.2 hicpp-no-assembler Rule 10.4.1 hicpp-multiway-paths-covered Rule 9.4.2 the safety profile adds WarnOnMissingElse for Rule 9.4.1 fuchsia-virtual-inheritance Rules 8.2.1, 13.1.1, 13.1.2 cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-union-access Rule 12.3.1 there are no unions cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-vararg Rules 8.2.11, 21.10.1 the Log hook takes a plain const char* ; host tests and examples that print may turn it off in their own folder cert-err34-c , cert-env33-c , cert-err52-cpp , cert-flp30-c Rules 21.2.1, 21.2.3, 21.10.2, Dir 0.3.1 through cert-* Safety level only, because they would fight idioms the standard and high levels accept (public value and error in Result , a deleted copy without a written-out move, byte-buffer arithmetic in tests, test helpers with external linkage) or are style the org does not use elsewhere: cppcoreguidelines-pro-bounds-array-to-pointer-decay , cppcoreguidelines-pro-bounds-pointer-arithmetic , cppcoreguidelines-special-member-functions , misc-non-private-member-variables-in-classes , misc-use-anonymous-namespace , misc-use-internal-linkage and the google-* checks ( build-namespaces , default-arguments , explicit-constructor , global-names-in-headers , readability-casting , runtime-int , runtime-operator ). Include guards (Rule 19.2.1) are decided by the handbook's own source check, not by llvm-header-guard , whose names are derived from the path and differ from the convention in KB-CPP-019 . What open tools can and cannot prove ¶ clang-tidy, cppcheck and the compilers decide a large part of MISRA and CERT, but not all of it: some guidelines are undecidable in general, and some decidable ones are only implemented by commercial checkers (Cppcheck Premium, Helix QAC, Parasoft C/C++test, Polyspace and others). The matrix never claims a guideline is checked by a tool that does not check it. At the safety level a commercial checker runs on every release, under the licence of the organisation qualifying the component, and its report becomes part of the evidence package. Copyright ¶ The MISRA and CERT documents are copyrighted. The handbook cites guideline numbers, categories and analysis attributes with our own one-line summaries; it does not reproduce headlines, rationale, examples or tables, and the standard itself is never committed to any repository. Contributors working at the safety level need their own licensed copies of the standards.

docs.text: Deviations and waivers ¶ A rule can be set aside, but never silently. There are two kinds of exception, and both are checked by CI. A deviation: one place in the code ¶ When a check flags code that is correct and deliberate, the finding is suppressed where it occurs, with the check named and the reason stated: // The not-in-range form is deliberate: a NaN fails every comparison, so it is rejected here. // NOLINTNEXTLINE(readability-simplify-boolean-expr) if ( ! ( value >= kMin && value <= kMax )) { At the standard level, the comment is the record. At the high and safety levels, every suppression also has an entry in docs/deviations.yml of the repository, which the conformance check compares with the suppressions in the code: an entry without a suppression, or a suppression without an entry, fails CI. - id : DEV-007 rule : KB-CPP-008 check : clang-tidy/readability-simplify-boolean-expr where : inc/xmpl100_types.hpp reason : The negated range test rejects NaN, which the rewritten form would accept. risk : None; the alternative is the defect. approved_by : "@N3b3x" date : 2026-11-06 This follows the deviation-record model of MISRA Compliance:2020: the guideline, the location, the justification, the consequence, and who accepted it. A project-wide MISRA deviation ¶ Some MISRA C++:2023 guidelines conflict with a decision the whole project has made, such as writing C++20 or reaching memory-mapped registers in the MCU port. Those are recorded once, in compliance/misra-cpp-2023-deviations.yml , and apply to every repository at the safety level: - id : MD-CPP-003 guideline : Rule 8.2.5 scope : Memory-mapped register access in MCU port and board bind code, and nowhere else. justification : A peripheral register is an object at a fixed address; reaching it needs a cast. mitigation : One named accessor per register block, volatile fixed-width types, a NOLINT citing MD-CPP-003. approved_by : maintainer date : 2026-11-08 review_by : 2027-11-08 Each record names one guideline, the scope it covers (everything outside the scope complies), the justification, the mitigation that keeps the guideline's risk under control, who approved it and when it must be reviewed again. The guideline's entry in the compliance matrix lists the record, and checks/misra_matrix.py fails CI if a record cites a guideline that does not exist or is mandatory, or if the matrix and the records disagree. A suppression in the code that a project-wide record covers cites the record's id instead of adding a per-repository entry. A waiver: a whole rule, for a while ¶ When a repository cannot meet a rule yet, it records a waiver in .kokeb/handbook.yml : waivers : - rule : KB-DOC-004 reason : Doxygen comments for the v2 register API land with #41. approved_by : "@N3b3x" until : 2027-01-31 The conformance check reports the waiver on every run, and fails once until has passed. A waiver is a dated promise, not a permanent exemption; a rule that a repository will never meet needs a decision record that changes the rule or its scope instead. What cannot be waived ¶ At the safety level, MISRA's mandatory guidelines and the evidence package cannot be waived (MISRA does not permit deviations from mandatory guidelines either). They can only be met, or the component's level lowered.

( value >= kMin && value <= kMax )) { At the standard level, the comment is the record. At the high and safety levels, every suppression also has an entry in docs/deviations.yml of the repository, which the conformance check compares with the suppressions in the code: an entry without a suppression, or a suppression without an entry, fails CI. - id : DEV-007 rule : KB-CPP-008 check : clang-tidy/readability-simplify-boolean-expr where : inc/xmpl100_types.hpp reason : The negated range test rejects NaN, which the rewritten form would accept. risk : None; the alternative is the defect. approved_by : "@N3b3x" date : 2026-11-06 This follows the deviation-record model of MISRA Compliance:2020: the guideline, the location, the justification, the consequence, and who accepted it.
docs.title: A deviation: one place in the code

docs.text: Some MISRA C++:2023 guidelines conflict with a decision the whole project has made, such as writing C++20 or reaching memory-mapped registers in the MCU port. Those are recorded once, in compliance/misra-cpp-2023-deviations.yml , and apply to every repository at the safety level: - id : MD-CPP-003 guideline : Rule 8.2.5 scope : Memory-mapped register access in MCU port and board bind code, and nowhere else. justification : A peripheral register is an object at a fixed address; reaching it needs a cast. mitigation : One named accessor per register block, volatile fixed-width types, a NOLINT citing MD-CPP-003. approved_by : maintainer date : 2026-11-08 review_by : 2027-11-08 Each record names one guideline, the scope it covers (everything outside the scope complies), the justification, the mitigation that keeps the guideline's risk under control, who approved it and when it must be reviewed again. The guideline's entry in the compliance matrix lists the record, and checks/misra_matrix.py fails CI if a record cites a guideline that does not exist or is mandatory, or if the matrix and the records disagree. A suppression in the code that a project-wide record covers cites the record's id instead of adding a per-repository entry.
docs.title: A project-wide MISRA deviation

docs.text: When a repository cannot meet a rule yet, it records a waiver in .kokeb/handbook.yml : waivers : - rule : KB-DOC-004 reason : Doxygen comments for the v2 register API land with #41. approved_by : "@N3b3x" until : 2027-01-31 The conformance check reports the waiver on every run, and fails once until has passed. A waiver is a dated promise, not a permanent exemption; a rule that a repository will never meet needs a decision record that changes the rule or its scope instead.
docs.title: A waiver: a whole rule, for a while

docs.text: At the safety level, MISRA's mandatory guidelines and the evidence package cannot be waived (MISRA does not permit deviations from mandatory guidelines either). They can only be met, or the component's level lowered.
docs.title: What cannot be waived

docs.text: Evidence for regulated products ¶ A team that puts a Kokeb component into a regulated product (a medical device, an industrial safety function, a vehicle) has to show its own regulator or assessor what the component is, how it was verified and what is known to be wrong with it. Each release of a high or safety component publishes that evidence, generated by CI from the same checks that guard every pull request, so it cannot drift from the code. What each release carries ¶ Item high safety Produced by Exact identification: version, commit, tag, build inputs ✓ ✓ release workflow Checksums ( SHA256SUMS ) and build provenance ✓ ✓ release workflow SBOM (SPDX) of everything the component contains or pulls in ✓ ✓ release workflow Rules that applied, and the result of every check ✓ ✓ conformance workflow Deviation records and active waivers ✓ ✓ conformance workflow Test report: every test, its result, on which compilers and targets ✓ ✓ host and cross builds Coverage report, lines and branches ✓ ✓ coverage job Static analysis results (clang-tidy, cppcheck) ✓ ✓ lint jobs Requirements and their trace to code and to tests ✓ traceability check Justification of every uncovered branch ✓ maintainers, checked for completeness MISRA compliance summary and the commercial checker's report ✓ compliance matrix and checker run Known anomalies: every open defect that affects the release, with its impact ✓ issue tracker export Signature over the whole package ✓ release workflow Requirements and traceability (safety) ¶ A safety component keeps its requirements in docs/requirements.yml , one entry per requirement with an ID ( REQ-<component>-NNN ), the statement, and its source (datasheet section, standard clause, or design decision). Code and tests point at requirement IDs in comments ( // Implements: REQ-XMPL100-012 , // Verifies: REQ-XMPL100-012 ). The traceability check fails when a requirement has no implementing code or no verifying test, or when code or a test cites an ID that does not exist. Known anomalies ¶ Open defects live as GitHub issues labelled bug . At release, the open ones that affect the released code are exported with their impact and workaround, which is what a manufacturer's evaluation of known anomalies in off-the-shelf software (IEC 62304 7.1.3) asks for.
docs.title: Evidence

docs.text: How rules work ¶ A rule is data ¶ Each rule lives in rules/<area>.yml and has: Field Meaning id KB-<AREA>-<NNN> , for example KB-CPP-003 . Never reused, never renumbered. HardFOC's supplement uses HF- . level must : CI or review fails without it. should : the pull request says why if it is not followed. guide : how we prefer to do it. applies The repository kinds it applies to ( driver , library , hal , firmware , tooling , docs , template , or all ) and the lowest assurance level it applies from. verify How it is verified: a check from the check registry , or review with the checklist line a reviewer confirms. status proposed (warns, with enforce_from ), active (enforced), or retired (kept so the ID is never reused). refs The decision record behind it, and the clauses of MISRA, CERT, the C++ Core Guidelines or IEC 62304 it corresponds to. The pages under Rules are generated from these files, and CI fails if they are stale, so the words you read are the data CI enforces. What makes a rule valid ¶ The handbook's own CI ( checks/handbook.py ) refuses: an active must rule with no check and no review line; a check that is not in the registry, or a registry entry marked implemented without saying where it runs; a duplicate or reused ID; a reference to a decision record, page or standard that does not exist. Every check in the registry is either implemented (it runs in a named workflow and fails on a finding) or planned . The coverage page counts both, so the gap between what we say and what we check is always visible. How a repository follows the handbook ¶ A repository declares, in .kokeb/handbook.yml : handbook : "1.0" # the handbook release it follows kind : driver level : high # standard | high | safety waivers : # see Deviations and waivers - rule : KB-DOC-004 reason : Doxygen comments for the v2 register API land with #41 approved_by : "@N3b3x" until : 2027-01-31 Its CI calls the conformance workflow, which runs every check that applies to its kind and level and reports each failure by rule ID, with the rule's text and a link here. People and agents see the same thing. How rules change ¶ A new must rule arrives as proposed with an enforce_from date: it warns until that date, then fails. Tightening or removing a rule needs a decision record. The handbook is released like code ( v1.0.0 , v1.1.0 , …). Repositories pin a minor version and move up on purpose, the way they pin ci-tools@v1 .
docs.title: How rules work

docs.text: IEC 62304 ¶ IEC 62304 ( Medical device software: software life cycle processes ) is the standard a medical device manufacturer follows for the software in its device. It applies to the manufacturer's process, not to a library on its own. This page explains how a Kokeb component fits into that process, so that a manufacturer can use one in software of any safety class, including class C. This page is general guidance, not regulatory advice. The manufacturer decides how a component is treated and remains responsible for the device. Two ways a manufacturer can use a Kokeb component ¶ As SOUP (software of unknown provenance): the component is used as released. The manufacturer identifies it, states the requirements it relies on, evaluates its published anomalies, and verifies it within their system. The evidence package gives them everything that needs. As their own software item : the manufacturer brings the component under their own process, for example by forking it at a release. The rules, tests, coverage, traceability and deviation records then become starting evidence for their own verification. How handbook mechanisms map onto the standard ¶ IEC 62304 clause What it asks of the manufacturer What a Kokeb component provides 5.1 Development planning Plans, standards, methods and tools This handbook: the rules, the coding standards, the named tools and their versions 5.2 Requirements analysis Software requirements docs/requirements.yml at the safety level 5.3 Architectural design Architecture, interfaces, SOUP requirements Standards pages and decision records; the Contract page of each driver; the SBOM 5.4 Detailed design Design of each unit (class C) Doxygen API reference generated from documented headers 5.5 Unit implementation and verification Unit verification process and acceptance criteria; additional criteria for class C Static analysis, host tests, sanitizers, coverage and the coding-standard matrix, all in CI ( KB-CPP-008 , KB-TST-001 ) 5.6 Integration and integration testing Integration testing Builds for every supported target; ESP-IDF and board examples 5.8 Release Known residual anomalies, archived, repeatable build Immutable tags, provenance, the anomaly list, reproducible CI builds 7.1 Risk analysis, SOUP Evaluate SOUP and its published anomalies The anomaly list in the evidence package 8 Configuration management Identify items and SOUP, control change Releases and tags ( KB-GIT-003 ), pull-request-only changes ( KB-GIT-002 ), the SBOM 9 Problem resolution Record, investigate and resolve problems GitHub issues and the security policy; fixes linked to releases in the changelog What stays with the manufacturer ¶ Safety classification, risk management (ISO 14971), system requirements, hazard analysis, system testing, clinical evaluation and the device's technical documentation. A Kokeb component supplies evidence for its own part; it cannot supply the device's.
docs.title: IEC 62304

docs.text: Architecture decision records ¶ Why the Kokeb Labs standard is what it is. Each record is one decision in the Context / Decision / Consequences form, numbered in the order it was accepted. A record is never edited to change its decision; a new record supersedes it, and the old one gets a Superseded by ADR-NNNN status. ADR Decision Status 0001 Drivers keep <chip>::Error and Result<T> ; handlers map to kb::Status Accepted 0002 One lifecycle: I/O-free constructor, Initialize() , EnsureInitialized() Accepted, amended by 0021 0003 Drivers are templates on a CRTP port constrained by a concept Accepted 0004 No heap in drivers; none after start-up anywhere Accepted 0005 A shared kb-hal-common repository; board HALs live with their products Accepted 0006 FreeRTOS at 1 kHz everywhere; a delay waits at least the requested time Accepted 0007 Drivers pinned in kb-core to release tags; driver.yml , catalog/compat.yml and release trains Accepted 0008 One naming scheme, enforced by clang-tidy Accepted 0009 MIT for firmware and tooling; CERN-OHL-P-2.0 for hardware designs Accepted 0010 C++20 in every repository Accepted 0011 The root holds only required and first-read files; tool configuration in _config/ ; platform code only in examples/<platform>/ Accepted 0012 Drivers carry no brand: driver-<chip> , namespace <chip> , <chip>::<chip> Accepted 0013 kb-core is one monorepo with four targets and one version Accepted 0014 Chip-, MCU- and product-specific code each have one place Accepted 0015 Governance for one maintainer, open to contributors Accepted 0016 Virtual functions only at the three run-time boundaries Accepted 0017 Target code uses a named subset of the standard library Accepted 0018 Commit sdkconfig.defaults , never the generated sdkconfig Accepted 0019 Datasheets are referenced by exact revision, never committed Accepted 0020 Complexity limits and coverage floors per assurance level Accepted 0021 EnsureInitialized() is the one start-up entry point Accepted Format ¶ # ADR-NNNN: <decision as a short sentence> - Status: Proposed | Accepted | Superseded by ADR-NNNN - Date: YYYY-MM-DD ## Context What forced a decision: the problem, the constraints, the options considered. ## Decision What we do, stated as rules. ## Consequences What gets better, what gets worse, and what has to change in which repositories. A new record is added in the same PR as the change to the standard it explains. It is proposed in a PR to kokeb-labs/.github and stays open for comment for at least seven days unless it fixes a defect. Where the decisions came from ¶ Records 0001 to 0011 were accepted on 3 November 2026, after a read-only review of the code the standard grew from (drivers, libraries, HALs and products) against one checklist: API shape, port, errors, start-up, config, memory and threading, naming, build, tests and docs. The review found the repository shell, docs and CI already uniform, and the C++ contracts not: 5 error models, 6 start-up styles, about 8 spellings of the same port hooks, two handler families, drifting HALs and about 45 error types. When the standard was set up for Kokeb Labs on 5 November 2026, those records were rewritten for the new org (names, licence, the kb-core layout), and records 0012 to 0015 were added. From then on, the rule at the top of this page applies. The order of work: Write it down : this standard, the org clang configs, kokeb-labs/driver-template and ci-tools . kb-core skeleton : utils with kb::Status , rtos , interfaces with ToStatus() , each its own target, with the MCU gate and catalog/compat.yml . Drivers , in parallel, each released as driver-<chip> with its driver.yml , and each landing with its kb-core handler. kb-core handlers on one family, with shared adapter bases. kb-hal-common : the shared managers, facade base, bind interface, lints and an example board HAL; board-hal-template after it. The first release train , then the STM32 compile job and bind.

docs.text: ADR-0001: Drivers keep their own error type; handlers map to kb::Status ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ The review this standard grew from found five error models across the drivers (success spelt Success , None , Ok and OK ; one driver bool -only; bitmask flags in another), about 30 more error types above them, and two incompatible ManagerError enums in the HALs that no product read. Bus errors were lost in several places: void UART writes, void GPIO hooks, a getter returning a stale angle after a failed read. Two shapes were considered: one shared kb::Result used everywhere including drivers, or a small per-driver Result<T> and Error mapped to a shared status at the handler. A shared type inside drivers would make every driver depend on kb-core, and the drivers are meant to be usable on any MCU without the rest of the stack. Decision ¶ Each driver declares enum class <chip>::Error : uint8_t with a fixed base set ( Ok , NotInitialized , InvalidArgument , Bus , Timeout , DeviceIdMismatch , Crc , Busy , DeviceFault , Unsupported , values 0 to 9), chip-specific values from 16, and <chip>::Result<T> with ok() and [[nodiscard]] . Above the drivers there is one status, kb::Status (12 codes), and one result, kb::Result<T> , carrying the original code as detail . They live in a dependency-free header in kb-core's utils ( kb/utils/Status.h ). Each boundary maps once: handlers map driver errors, the interfaces map kb_*_err_t with ToStatus() , the facade adds the failing manager, the product maps to its fault catalogue. Consequences ¶ Drivers stay standalone and keep precise, chip-level errors. One mapping table serves every handler because the base set has fixed values. Every driver whose API returns bool or flags changes its public API once, before v0.1. ManagerError enums and per-layer error types do not exist. detail keeps the original code for diagnostics, but code above the handler cannot branch on it.

docs.text: ADR-0002: One lifecycle for drivers and handlers ¶ Status: Accepted; the driver and handler parts amended by ADR-0021 Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ The review found six start-up styles. Some drivers had no initialisation at all, one reset the chip the first time any setter ran, some constructors did I/O, and handlers either built their driver with make_unique in an Initialize() or exposed only EnsureInitialized() . A caller could not tell when the bus was first touched or whether a failed start-up could be retried. Decision ¶ Constructors are noexcept , do no I/O and cannot fail. Drivers have Initialize(const Config& = {}) : port up, reset, chip-ID check, apply config; then EnsureInitialized() , IsInitialized() and Deinitialize() . Every I/O call returns NotInitialized before initialisation; nothing initialises as a side effect. Handlers have EnsureInitialized() returning kb::Result<void> , which emplaces the driver in place and runs its initialisation, and leaves nothing cached on failure so the next call retries. HAL managers have Initialize() / Deinitialize() ; the facade starts them in a fixed order and fails closed. Consequences ¶ Construction order no longer matters: objects can be static, and the bus is first touched at a known point. A missing chip is a DeviceIdMismatch / NotFound at start-up instead of garbage later. Drivers without initialisation gain one; drivers that reset on first use stop doing so.
docs.title: ADR-0002: One lifecycle for drivers and handlers

docs.text: ADR-0003: Drivers are templates on a CRTP port ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ Most drivers in the review already used a CRTP port with no virtual functions, but with about eight spellings of the same hooks ( transfer , write_some and others), five base-class names, and void , int or bool returns. Optional hooks were detected with void_t in some repositories and requires in others, and one driver silently skipped required delays when its port had no delay hook. A base class that forwards a hook to the derived class turns a missing override into infinite recursion. Decision ¶ The port base is <chip>::{Spi,I2c,Uart,Adc}Interface<Derived> , non-copyable, with a protected constructor and no virtual functions. The driver template is constrained by a concept <chip>::{Spi,I2c,Uart,Adc}Port . Required hooks are PascalCase, noexcept , return bool , move raw bytes only, and are not declared in the base. Optional hooks ( DelayUs , DelayMs , GpioSet , GpioRead , Log ) are detected with C++20 requires in one helper; a missing hook falls back in a documented way or fails to compile. Pins are logical ( CtrlPin , GpioSignal::ACTIVE ); the port maps them to the board. Run-time polymorphism starts at the Base* interfaces in kb-core's interfaces , which the handler's adapter calls. Consequences ¶ No virtual calls or vtables in drivers; the port is inlined. A wrong or missing hook is a compile error with a readable message. Every port, in kb-core adapters, examples and user code, uses the standard hooks. Register-addressed I2C hooks become raw Write / WriteRead .

docs.text: ADR-0004: No heap in drivers, none after start-up anywhere ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ Embedded targets run for months; heap fragmentation and allocation failure after start-up are hard to test and hard to recover from. The review found a driver documented as heap-free that allocated, std::function in two drivers, a static report buffer in another, handlers allocating with make_unique and nothrow new , and wrappers returned as std::shared_ptr . Decision ¶ Drivers use no heap, exceptions, RTTI, std::function , std::string , printf or static mutable state. Callbacks are a function pointer plus void* . Handlers store their driver in place ( std::optional ) and their wrappers in fixed arrays. HALs and products allocate only during start-up, for objects that live until reset, and the HAL allocation lint lists them. Nothing allocates after start-up. Every repository builds with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti . Consequences ¶ Memory use is visible at link time and does not change at run time. APIs that returned owning pointers or shared_ptr change to references into fixed storage. Capacity limits become constexpr constants that a board can size, and "pool full" is Status::NoMemory .

docs.text: ADR-0005: A shared kb-hal-common repository ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ Board HALs that start as copies of each other drift: in the review, six managers were near-copies, the facades were near-clones, the platform binds used different shapes and verbs, each HAL's lint missed the other's rules, and their ManagerError enums differed in values, width and namespace. Keeping copies aligned by hand was the alternative; the drift shows it does not hold. Board HALs are also product code: their pin tables, chip lists and board-specific managers belong to one product. Decision ¶ kb-hal-common in kokeb-labs (namespace kb::hal ) holds ManagerBase , FacadeBase with ordered, fail-closed start-up and one CollectDiagnostics() , the six common managers (NVS, LED, GPIO, ADC, temperature, comms), one PlatformBind interface, the lints, and an example board HAL. Board HALs live in the product's organization or repository. A board HAL keeps only its board config, its pin table (written with the generic pincfg framework), its bind and its board-specific managers. kb-hal-common is a submodule of each board HAL, pinned to a release tag. kokeb-labs/board-hal-template will carry the board HAL shell; until it exists, new board HALs start from the example in kb-hal-common . Consequences ¶ A fix to a common manager lands once. A new board starts from kb-hal-common and the new-board checklist instead of a copy. One more repository to release, between kb-core and the board HALs in the release order. The common managers take everything board-specific as configuration and never name a board.

docs.text: ADR-0006: FreeRTOS runs at 1 kHz everywhere ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ ESP-IDF defaults to a 100 Hz tick. A millisecond delay rounds up to whole ticks, so at 100 Hz a 1 ms wait becomes 10 ms or more, which breaks datasheet timing in drivers and any 1 kHz control or CANopen loop. Some projects had set 1000 Hz and some had not. Decision ¶ Every FreeRTOS project (products, board HALs, kb-core, every driver's examples/esp32 ) sets CONFIG_FREERTOS_HZ=1000 in sdkconfig.defaults (and in a committed sdkconfig , while any remain). Milliseconds are converted with pdMS_TO_TICKS() or the kb::rtos helpers, never as raw tick counts; tick deadlines are compared by signed subtraction. A delay waits at least the requested time: the conversion rounds up and adds one tick. ThreadX builds use a 1 kHz kernel tick as well. Consequences ¶ One millisecond means one millisecond, give or take one tick, on every board and example. Ten times as many tick interrupts as the ESP-IDF default, a small and fixed CPU cost. pdMS_TO_TICKS() overflows above about 71 minutes and the tick counter wraps after about 49.7 days; code that waits that long uses kb::MonotonicUs() instead. The templates set the tick for every new project.

docs.text: ADR-0007: Drivers pinned in kb-core to release tags; tested sets released as trains ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03, updated 2026-11-05 Context ¶ The stack is composed with Git submodules. Without tags, declared versions drift apart and a board cannot report which versions it runs. The ESP-IDF component registry was considered: most drivers are not IDF components, the HALs include kb-core through CMake, and the host and STM32 builds need a non-IDF path. Independent driver versions also leave users asking which combination works. They need named, tested sets, and the build needs to know which drivers work on which MCU. Decision ¶ kb-core includes each driver as a submodule in drivers/driver-<chip>/ , pinned to a release tag commit ( vX.Y.Z , or vX.Y.Z-rc.N during a wave). Board HALs and products pin kb-core and kb-hal-common the same way. Each driver has independent SemVer starting at 0.1.0 ; kb-core has one version for all its parts. Each driver describes itself in driver.yml (bus, supported MCUs, peripheral, minimum kb-core). kb-core builds catalog/compat.yml from the pinned drivers' files; it is kb-core's bill of materials and generates the MCU gate table in cmake/kb_build_settings.cmake . A future kb command-line tool and a web configurator read it too. A tested set of one kb-core version and its pinned drivers is a release train, named kb YYYY.N . Board HALs and products carry version_lock.txt ( REF_<repo>=vX.Y.Z@<sha> ), checked in CI: a warning on PRs to main , a failure on release/* and tag pushes, plus a check that the tag is on main . Firmware reports the train and the tag and SHA of every submodule. Releases go bottom-up, each layer re-pinned to the tags below it. Consequences ¶ A product release names exactly what it contains, all the way down, and a user can pick a train instead of choosing driver versions one by one. Enabling a driver on an MCU it does not support fails at CMake configure time. Moving a driver forward is a pin PR in kb-core; a bump bot opens them. Private product repositories are not protected by tag rulesets on the free plan; the CI pin and ancestry checks are their only safeguard. The registry can be revisited for outside users once 0.x settles.

docs.text: ADR-0008: One naming scheme, enforced by clang-tidy ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ The review found methods in PascalCase, camelCase and snake_case; units written _mA , _ma , Ma , Mv , Ua or as a Unit enum; symbols declared at global scope; driver classes named Device or Driver ; and diverging .clang-format files (column limit 100 in most, 120 in some) and .clang-tidy files with no naming rules. Decision ¶ Namespaces: <chip> for drivers, kb for kb-core, kb::hal for the shared HAL, <board> for board code, <board>::app for products. Drivers carry no org prefix ( ADR-0012 ). Types, functions and public methods PascalCase; private methods camelBack; variables and parameters snake_case; private members snake_case_ ; constants kPascalCase ; macros UPPER_CASE ; units as suffixes; Read* for calls that touch the bus. Datasheet names may stay UPPER_CASE . One include root per repository or kb-core part ( kb/interfaces/BaseSpi.h ). One org .clang-format (LLVM base, 100 columns) and one .clang-tidy with readability-identifier-naming , kept in kokeb-labs/.github/standards/config/ and copied unchanged into each repository's _config/ . Consequences ¶ Names are predictable across the stack, and a reviewer no longer argues style. Private helpers stay camelBack, which register-level drivers already use, so they pass with few findings. Code brought in at 120 columns reformats once, in a PR that changes nothing else. Public API renames (camelCase methods, unit spellings) are breaking changes and land with the v0.1 API work.

docs.text: ADR-0009: MIT for firmware and tooling; CERN-OHL-P-2.0 for hardware designs ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03, updated 2026-11-05 Context ¶ Kokeb Labs publishes drivers, libraries, tooling and, later, hardware designs as open source, and wants them used in products, including closed ones, without a licence question. Mixed licences complicate kb-core and firmware images, which combine many drivers into one binary. Hardware designs need a licence written for hardware. Decision ¶ Every firmware, library, driver and tooling repository is MIT, with the MIT text in LICENSE and MIT in the README and any package metadata. Hardware designs (schematics, layouts, mechanical files) are CERN-OHL-P-2.0, the permissive variant, with the licence text in that repository's LICENSE . Contributions come in under the repository's licence with a DCO sign-off; there is no CLA ( ADR-0015 ). The licences cover the work, not the Kokeb Labs name or logos; those are covered by the trademark policy . Consequences ¶ One licence for all code and every firmware image; products can use it without releasing their own code. Code copied in from elsewhere must be MIT compatible; third-party code keeps its own licence in third_party/ with its notice. A fork may use the code freely but not the name; unbranded drivers make that easy.

docs.text: ADR-0010: C++20 in every repository ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ Part of the code the standard was built from was C++17 and the rest C++20. The standard relies on C++20: requires expressions for optional port hooks, concepts for port constraints, std::span for caller buffers, designated initialisers for configs. ESP-IDF 5.x and current STM32 toolchains support C++20. Decision ¶ Every repository builds as C++20 ( target_compile_features(<target> PUBLIC cxx_std_20) , Standard: c++20 in .clang-format ). Public headers may use any C++20 language feature the pinned ESP-IDF GCC and the CI clang both support; library features are limited to the freestanding-friendly headers listed in layers.md . Consequences ¶ One feature set for every repository; void_t detection and SFINAE tricks are replaced by requires . Users of a driver need a C++20 compiler. C++17 code moves up when it is brought in, which is compatible for callers already on C++20.

docs.text: ADR-0011: Repository root layout ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-03 Context ¶ A driver template whose root held about twenty entries ( Doxyfile , mkdocs.yml , Kconfig , idf_component.yml , .clang-format and .clang-tidy as symlinks into _config/ , CONTRIBUTING.md , SECURITY.md and TEMPLATE.md next to the README) did not let a reader see at a glance what a repository is, and the symlinks hid where the real configuration lived: two names for one file, broken on Windows checkouts, and easy to edit in the wrong place. Tool configuration was split between the root and _config/ with no rule for which went where. ESP-IDF support was a wrapper component under examples/esp32/components/ that sourced the root Kconfig and the build settings, plus a root idf_component.yml that no release used: the component manager does not need a manifest for a git dependency, and the stack does not publish to the ESP Component Registry. The layout also read as if the drivers were ESP32 drivers, though their code is MCU-agnostic and ESP32 is only the first example platform. Decision ¶ The root holds only (a) files GitHub or a tool requires at the root, and (b) the files a reader looks for first. For a driver or standalone library repository that is: Files: README.md , LICENSE , CHANGELOG.md , CMakeLists.txt , AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , .gitignore , .gitmodules , and driver.yml in a driver (its metadata, read by kb-core's catalog). Folders: .github/ , .claude/ , _config/ , cmake/ , docs/ , examples/ , inc/ , src/ , tests/ , tools/ . Other kinds keep their own source folders (kb-core: utils/ , rtos/ , interfaces/ , handlers/ , drivers/ , catalog/ ; kb-hal-common : include/ , lib/ , templates/ ) and add only what a tool requires at the root, named in their AGENTS.md (for example CMakePresets.json , which CMake reads only from the source root). 2. One location for tool configuration: _config/ . clang-format, clang-tidy, Doxyfile , mkdocs.yml ( docs_dir: ../docs ), Kconfig , markdownlint, yamllint and lychee live there. Every command and workflow names the path ( --style=file:_config/.clang-format , --config-file=_config/.clang-tidy , mkdocs build -f _config/mkdocs.yml , mkdocs_config / doxygen_config in the docs workflow). Doxygen runs from the root, so paths inside _config/Doxyfile stay relative to the root. 3. No symlinks. Editors that find .clang-format / .clang-tidy only by name use a local copy that .gitignore lists; nothing at the root is a link. 4. CONTRIBUTING.md and SECURITY.md live in .github/ , where GitHub reads them as well. 5. One root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Under ESP_PLATFORM it is the ESP-IDF component ( idf_component_register() from cmake/<chip>_build_settings.cmake , KCONFIG _config/Kconfig ); otherwise it is the CMake library with the <chip>::<chip> alias and install/export. An ESP-IDF project uses the repository directly: EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS , a checkout under components/ , or a component-manager git dependency. There is no root idf_component.yml and no example wrapper component. A manifest is added only if registry publishing is chosen. This ESP_PLATFORM branch is build glue; source files never test ESP_PLATFORM ( ADR-0014 ). 6. Drivers and libraries are MCU-agnostic. Platform code lives only in examples/<platform>/ , one self-contained folder per platform carrying its own port, built by CI. Every repository ships examples/host/ , which runs on any PC and is built and run in the host tests. Plain CMake covers STM32, RP2040, nRF and host builds; Zephyr, Arduino or PlatformIO manifests are added only when a user needs them, without a second copy of the sources. kb-core's interfaces/mcu/<family>/ and board HALs, which are MCU-specific by design through their binds, are the documented exceptions. Consequences ¶ A reader sees the README, the licence, the changelog and the build entry point, and every configuration is in one obvious place. The template's setup self-test fails when a generated root holds anything else. Tools are called with a path. The lint workflow takes clang_format_config / clang_tidy_config ; the docs tooling ( kokeb-docs ) takes the folder that holds docs_dir as the repository root, finds _config/mkdocs.yml on its own and accepts kokeb-docs -f . ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so a project that uses EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS on a checkout requires the checkout folder's name; a submodule under components/<chip> or a component-manager key gives a stable name. Room for more platforms without touching the root: a new examples/<platform>/ with its CI job, and a manifest only when a build system cannot use the root CMakeLists.txt .

The layout also read as if the drivers were ESP32 drivers, though their code is MCU-agnostic and ESP32 is only the first example platform.
docs.title: Context

docs.text: The root holds only (a) files GitHub or a tool requires at the root, and (b) the files a reader looks for first. For a driver or standalone library repository that is: Files: README.md , LICENSE , CHANGELOG.md , CMakeLists.txt , AGENTS.md , CLAUDE.md , .gitignore , .gitmodules , and driver.yml in a driver (its metadata, read by kb-core's catalog). Folders: .github/ , .claude/ , _config/ , cmake/ , docs/ , examples/ , inc/ , src/ , tests/ , tools/ . Other kinds keep their own source folders (kb-core: utils/ , rtos/ , interfaces/ , handlers/ , drivers/ , catalog/ ; kb-hal-common : include/ , lib/ , templates/ ) and add only what a tool requires at the root, named in their AGENTS.md (for example CMakePresets.json , which CMake reads only from the source root). 2. One location for tool configuration: _config/ . clang-format, clang-tidy, Doxyfile , mkdocs.yml ( docs_dir: ../docs ), Kconfig , markdownlint, yamllint and lychee live there. Every command and workflow names the path ( --style=file:_config/.clang-format , --config-file=_config/.clang-tidy , mkdocs build -f _config/mkdocs.yml , mkdocs_config / doxygen_config in the docs workflow). Doxygen runs from the root, so paths inside _config/Doxyfile stay relative to the root. 3. No symlinks. Editors that find .clang-format / .clang-tidy only by name use a local copy that .gitignore lists; nothing at the root is a link. 4. CONTRIBUTING.md and SECURITY.md live in .github/ , where GitHub reads them as well. 5. One root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Under ESP_PLATFORM it is the ESP-IDF component ( idf_component_register() from cmake/<chip>_build_settings.cmake , KCONFIG _config/Kconfig ); otherwise it is the CMake library with the <chip>::<chip> alias and install/export. An ESP-IDF project uses the repository directly: EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS , a checkout under components/ , or a component-manager git dependency. There is no root idf_component.yml and no example wrapper component. A manifest is added only if registry publishing is chosen. This ESP_PLATFORM branch is build glue; source files never test ESP_PLATFORM ( ADR-0014 ). 6. Drivers and libraries are MCU-agnostic. Platform code lives only in examples/<platform>/ , one self-contained folder per platform carrying its own port, built by CI. Every repository ships examples/host/ , which runs on any PC and is built and run in the host tests. Plain CMake covers STM32, RP2040, nRF and host builds; Zephyr, Arduino or PlatformIO manifests are added only when a user needs them, without a second copy of the sources. kb-core's interfaces/mcu/<family>/ and board HALs, which are MCU-specific by design through their binds, are the documented exceptions.
docs.title: Decision

docs.text: A reader sees the README, the licence, the changelog and the build entry point, and every configuration is in one obvious place. The template's setup self-test fails when a generated root holds anything else. Tools are called with a path. The lint workflow takes clang_format_config / clang_tidy_config ; the docs tooling ( kokeb-docs ) takes the folder that holds docs_dir as the repository root, finds _config/mkdocs.yml on its own and accepts kokeb-docs -f . ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so a project that uses EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS on a checkout requires the checkout folder's name; a submodule under components/<chip> or a component-manager key gives a stable name. Room for more platforms without touching the root: a new examples/<platform>/ with its CI job, and a manifest only when a build system cannot use the root CMakeLists.txt .

docs.text: ADR-0012: Drivers carry no brand ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-05 Context ¶ A chip driver is the part of the stack most likely to be used alone: in another framework, on another MCU, or in a fork. An org prefix in its repository name, namespace, CMake target, macros or Kconfig symbols ( xx_<chip> , xx::<chip> , XX_<CHIP>_* ) ties it to the org for no technical reason. A fork either keeps a brand it has no right to, or renames every symbol and breaks its users. Two drivers for the same chip from different sources would also collide on the chip name only, which is the collision that matters. Decision ¶ A driver repository is driver-<chip> ( driver-pcal95555 ). Its namespace is <chip>:: only; its class is <chip>::<CHIP> ; its umbrella header is inc/<chip>.hpp . CMake: find_package(<chip>) , target <chip>::<chip> , build settings in cmake/<chip>_build_settings.cmake , options and macros <CHIP>_* . Kconfig: CONFIG_<CHIP>_* . A driver contains no kb_ , kb:: , KB_ , or any other org prefix, and depends on nothing in kb-core. The one mention of kb-core is kb_core_min in driver.yml , which is metadata. The kb prefix belongs to kb-core and kb-hal-common only. Consequences ¶ A driver is usable and forkable on its own; a fork inherits no brand and needs no renames. The trademark policy is easy to follow: the code carries no name to remove. kb-core's handlers refer to drivers by chip name ( pcal95555::PCAL95555 , pcal95555::pcal95555 ), which reads the same in every project. Two packages for the same chip cannot be installed side by side under the same prefix; that is accepted, since a project uses one driver per chip.

docs.text: ADR-0013: kb-core is one monorepo with four targets and one version ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-05 Context ¶ The code the standard was built from split the core into many repositories: separate utilities, an RTOS wrapper, an MCU interface wrapper, a pin-config library, aggregator repositories that only collected submodules, and the core with the handlers. Every change to a low layer took a chain of pin bumps through the aggregators; versions had to be kept compatible by hand; and headers with the same name in two repositories collided. The parts are tightly coupled and always released together. Users still need to take only part of it, for example the utilities on their own. Decision ¶ kb-core is one repository holding utils/ ( general , canopen ), rtos/ , interfaces/ ( base/ and mcu/esp32 , mcu/stm32 , mcu/host ), handlers/ ( common , one folder per chip), and drivers/driver-<chip>/ as git submodules pinned to driver release tags, with cmake/kb_build_settings.cmake and catalog/compat.yml . It exports four CMake targets that are consumable separately: kb::utils , kb::rtos , kb::interfaces , kb::handlers . Each is also installable as its own package. The dependency direction is fixed: utils ← rtos ← interfaces ← handlers . Drivers depend on nothing in kb-core. kb-core has one version number for all of its parts. Prefix: namespace kb:: , macros KB_ , includes "kb/..." , options KB_MCU=ESP32|STM32|HOST|NONE , KB_RTOS=FREERTOS|THREADX|NONE , KB_ENABLE_<CHIP> . Drivers stay separate repositories ( ADR-0012 ). Board HALs stay with their products ( ADR-0005 ). Consequences ¶ A change across utils, rtos, interfaces and handlers is one PR, tested together. No aggregator repositories and no pin chains inside the core; a driver update is one pin PR in kb-core. Upward includes fail to link because each part is its own target. A user who needs only kb::utils still clones kb-core (or installs the kb_utils package); that is accepted. The rtos layer supports FreeRTOS, ThreadX and none; other RTOS backends need a new ADR.

docs.text: ADR-0014: Chip-, MCU- and product-specific code each have one place ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-05 Context ¶ "Platform-specific" was used for three different things: code that knows one chip, code that knows one MCU, and code that knows one product. Treating them alike let MCU calls and #ifdef ESP_PLATFORM blocks spread into shared code, and let one product's needs (its pins, its channels, its limits) end up in drivers and the core, where every other product then carried them. Decision ¶ Kind Where it lives Rule Chip-specific Its own driver and its handler Fine there MCU-specific Only interfaces/mcu/<family>/ in kb-core (above core: a board HAL's bind, a product's platform/ ) The build selects the family and compiles only that folder; each header there #error s in any other build Product-specific The product's board HAL or repository Never in kb-core or a driver KB_MCU selects the family. Drivers that need one MCU's peripheral are listed in an MCU gate table in cmake/kb_build_settings.cmake ( "WS2812:ESP32:RMT" ), so enabling them on another MCU stops CMake. Differences between chip variants of one family use the vendor's capability macros, only inside mcu/<family>/ . Shared code never tests ESP_PLATFORM or a similar platform macro. Product needs become generic extension points: config masks, profile tables passed in, backend interfaces, injected loggers. The test for a change to kb-core or a driver: could a second, made-up product with a different board use it without editing core? Consequences ¶ Shared code compiles for every family and on the host, and a lint can check it by searching for platform macros. A wrong MCU for a driver is a configure error, not a link error or a bench surprise. Some product requests take longer, because the generic extension point has to be designed first. A peripheral only one family has gets a Base* interface and one implementation, which is more code than a direct call but keeps the call sites portable.

docs.text: ADR-0015: Governance for one maintainer, open to contributors ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-05 Context ¶ Kokeb Labs has one maintainer and wants outside contributions. Rules written for a team (one approving review on every PR) block a single maintainer from merging their own work, and the usual workaround, a bypass, removes the checks along with the review. Without a review, the remaining safeguards have to come from the rulesets and CI. Contributors also need to know under what terms their code comes in, without the friction of a CLA. Decision ¶ main changes only through PRs, squash-merged, with linear history and signed commits; GitHub signs the squash commit it creates. The required check is CI gate / gate . Conversations must be resolved before merge. main cannot be force-pushed or deleted; v* tags are protected. While there is one maintainer, PRs need 0 approvals and the owner merges their own PRs through a PR. When a second maintainer joins, PRs need one approving review from a code owner, and CODEOWNERS moves to the maintainers team. Contributions are accepted under the repository's licence with a DCO Signed-off-by: on every commit, checked by CI as part of the gate. There is no CLA. Vulnerabilities are reported privately through GitHub private vulnerability reporting. The code is MIT, but the Kokeb Labs name and logos are not licensed by it; a trademark policy covers them. Consequences ¶ The maintainer works under the same rules as contributors; nothing needs a bypass. Every change on main is a signed, single, revertable commit with a green gate. Without a second reviewer, CI and the checklists carry more of the review; safety-relevant changes get the safety label and a careful self-review. Adding a maintainer is a ruleset and CODEOWNERS change, not a new process.

docs.text: ADR-0016: Virtual functions only at the three run-time boundaries ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-06 Context ¶ The standard said two different things. The library page said Base* interfaces are "the one place above the bind with virtual functions", while the HAL page defines ManagerBase with pure virtual functions and a virtual CollectDiagnostics(DiagnosticsSink&) , and kb-core's BaseThread is a base class products derive from. A rule that the code already breaks cannot be enforced, and a checker needs one list it can test against. Decision ¶ Virtual functions are allowed in exactly three places, each a boundary where the concrete type is chosen when the board or product is built, not when the library is written: the Base* peripheral interfaces in kb-core's interfaces/base/ (the MCU boundary); kb-hal-common's ManagerBase , FacadeBase and the sink interfaces they take, such as DiagnosticsSink (the board boundary); kb-core's BaseThread and BaseThreadsManager (the task boundary). Everywhere else, including every driver, port, handler and utility, there are no virtual functions; ports use CRTP (ADR-0003). A class at a boundary is abstract, is never deleted through a base pointer (there is no heap after start-up, ADR-0004), and declares either a public virtual or a protected non-virtual destructor (C++ Core Guidelines C.35). The repositories that own a boundary list its folders in .kokeb/handbook.yml , and the forbidden-patterns/virtual-outside-interfaces check rejects virtual anywhere else. Consequences ¶ The library page's sentence is corrected to name all three boundaries; rule KB-ARCH-011 says the same. Adding a fourth boundary needs a new decision record, not a quiet exception.

docs.text: ADR-0017: Target code uses a named subset of the standard library ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-06 Context ¶ The layers page and ADR-0010 call the headers a driver may include "the freestanding subset". They are not: in C++20, <array> , <span> , <optional> , <cstring> , <cmath> and <algorithm> are hosted headers, available on every embedded toolchain we use but not freestanding by the standard's definition. A rule named after a standard term it contradicts invites argument about which list applies, and no tool can check "freestanding-friendly". Decision ¶ The term is the target library subset : the standard headers code that runs on a microcontroller may use. It is an allow-list, not a description. Drivers may include exactly the headers in the Driver row of the include table on the Layers page ( <cstdint> , <cstddef> , <array> , <algorithm> , <type_traits> , <concepts> , <limits> , <cmath> , <cstring> , <span> , <utility> , <optional> , <bit> ), plus <cstdarg> for the optional Log hook. Other target code (kb-core, HALs, firmware) may also include <atomic> , <chrono> (types and arithmetic; clocks come from kb::rtos ), <string_view> , <variant> , <tuple> , <iterator> , <numeric> , <new> (placement new only) and <cstdio> for snprintf into a caller's buffer. No target code includes a header that allocates, throws or needs an operating system: <string> , <vector> , <map> , <set> , the <unordered_*> and <list> / <deque> containers, <memory> , <functional> , <iostream> and the other stream headers, <thread> , <mutex> , <condition_variable> , <future> , <regex> , <filesystem> , <locale> , <exception> , <stdexcept> , <typeinfo> , <any> . Algorithms that may allocate ( std::stable_sort , std::stable_partition , std::inplace_merge ) are not used. Host-only tests and tools are exempt. The include-allowlist/driver and include-allowlist/target checks test each translation unit against these lists. Consequences ¶ The layers page and ADR-0010 say "target library subset" instead of "freestanding". Adding a header to the subset is a change to this record and to the include table.

docs.text: ADR-0018: Commit sdkconfig.defaults, never the generated sdkconfig ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-06 Context ¶ The driver and product pages say a full sdkconfig is not committed, but the threading page still describes projects that commit one, and the release page attaches sdkconfig to product releases. A committed sdkconfig silently overrides the defaults files, so the 1 kHz tick (ADR-0006) and any other required setting can be lost in a repository that commits one. Decision ¶ An ESP-IDF project commits sdkconfig.defaults (and sdkconfig.defaults.<target> where a target needs its own settings). Every setting the project depends on is in those files. The generated sdkconfig is in .gitignore and never committed. tracked-files/sdkconfig fails CI if one is tracked. A firmware release attaches the effective sdkconfig the build produced, so the exact configuration of the released binary is recorded without being a source of truth in the repository. Consequences ¶ The threading page's note about committed sdkconfig files becomes a migration step: delete it, and move any setting it held into sdkconfig.defaults . A reproducible build depends only on the defaults files and the pinned ESP-IDF version.

docs.text: ADR-0019: Datasheets are referenced by exact revision, never committed ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-06 Context ¶ The new-driver checklist said to store the datasheet in docs/datasheet/ "where its licence allows", while the driver template, the pull-request template and the agents page say no vendor PDF is committed. Vendor licences rarely allow redistribution and change over time, and a repository cannot tell which licence applied when a file was added. What reviewers and auditors actually need is to know exactly which revision the code was written against. Decision ¶ No datasheet, reference manual or application note is committed to a Kokeb Labs repository. tracked-files/datasheets fails CI on a tracked PDF under docs/ that is listed as vendor documentation. Each driver lists the documents it was written against in docs/datasheets.yml : vendor, title, document number, revision, date, the vendor's URL, and the SHA-256 of the PDF that was used. docs.text: ADR-0020: Complexity limits and coverage floors per assurance level ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-06 Context ¶ The handbook asked for "a coverage floor" without saying how coverage is measured, and had no rule on code complexity at all. Both are among the first things a safety assessor asks about, and both are meaningless without a fixed tool, a fixed definition and a number that is defended in writing. Decision ¶ Complexity ¶ Measured by lizard on library code ( inc/ , src/ , kb-core and HAL sources; not tests or examples), using the modified cyclomatic complexity, which counts a whole switch as one decision: a flat enum-to-string table is not branching logic a reader has to hold in their head. Limit per function standard high safety Cyclomatic complexity (modified) 15 15 10 Length (lines of code, without blanks and comments) 80 60 60 Parameters 7 6 6 Ten is McCabe's original limit, and NIST SP 500-235 recommends it, allowing up to 15 for experienced teams with a review of each case. Sixty lines is the NASA/JPL Power of Ten limit (one printed page). A function over a limit that is genuinely clearer as one piece, for example a state machine's transition table, has a deviation record (see Deviations); it is never split just to satisfy the number. Coverage ¶ Measured by gcovr over the host tests built with the pinned GCC at -O0 --coverage , counting only library code (as above), with unreachable branches and branches the compiler adds for exceptions excluded (we do not use exceptions). Compile-only targets that never run are not part of the measurement. Floor (library code) standard high safety Lines reported 85% 100% of reachable lines Branches reported 75% 100% of reachable branches MC/DC (GCC condition coverage) not measured reported 100% At the safety level, every line, branch or condition the tests do not reach is listed in docs/coverage-justification.yml with the reason (for example, a defensive check that the hardware cannot trigger, verified by review) and who accepted it. The coverage check fails when an unreached item has no justification, or a justification names an item the tests now reach. MC/DC uses GCC's -fcondition-coverage , which measures whether each condition in a decision independently affects its outcome. Test quality ¶ Coverage shows what ran, not what was checked. At the safety level, mutation testing (for example Mull) runs on each release and its surviving mutants are reviewed; this is guidance until the tooling is proven on our code base. Consequences ¶ Rules KB-CPP-115 (complexity), KB-TST-004 (coverage floors) and KB-TST-027 to 029 encode these numbers. ci-tools gains a reusable workflow that runs lizard, gcovr and the sanitizers and fails on these limits. Raising a floor is a minor handbook release with an enforce_from date; lowering one needs a new record.

docs.text: ADR-0021: EnsureInitialized() is the one start-up entry point ¶ Status: Accepted Date: 2026-11-07 Amends: ADR-0002 (the driver and handler parts) Context ¶ ADR-0002 gave drivers two public ways to start: Initialize(config) and EnsureInitialized() . Moving the first drivers showed what that costs: Initialize() can be called again on a running chip. It then resets and reconfigures it, for no reason and in the middle of operation, and nothing in the API discourages it. Two entry points with different behaviour on the second call are two contracts to test, document and review in every driver and every handler. Handlers will be singletons that own hardware and are used from several tasks. They need exactly one idempotent start, with no way to start twice. The handler standard also allowed a handler method to start the chip itself on first use. That hides start-up traffic (for the AS5047U, 42 SPI frames including writes) inside whatever call comes first, possibly a read in a control loop, and turns a start-up failure into the error of a read. Decision ¶ Drivers ¶ The constructor takes the port, any bus argument, and the configuration last with a default: explicit Chip(Port& port, ..., const Config& config = {}) noexcept . It stores them, does no I/O and cannot fail. EnsureInitialized() is the only public way to start. Its first call validates the stored configuration ( InvalidArgument , no I/O), brings the port up, resets and identifies the chip and applies the configuration, and only then marks the driver initialised. Once it has succeeded, later calls return Ok at once with no I/O. After a failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning. The start-up sequence itself is a private member ( initialize() ). There is no public Initialize() . Deinitialize() puts the chip in its safe state and marks the driver uninitialised. Recovery after a fault is Deinitialize() then EnsureInitialized() . ApplyConfig(config) validates first. On a running driver it writes the configuration; before the start it only stores it for the first EnsureInitialized() , with no I/O. No read or write starts the chip. Before EnsureInitialized() has succeeded, every call that needs the chip returns NotInitialized and sends nothing. A read is always the bus traffic it needs and nothing more. Handlers ¶ EnsureInitialized() is the handler's one start-up entry point too: it builds the driver in place and calls the driver's EnsureInitialized() , and on failure destroys it again so the next call retries. Handler reads and writes do not call EnsureInitialized() . They return NotInitialized until the handler has been started. The HAL starts its handlers once, in its fixed start-up order (ADR-0002), and a task that uses a handler before then gets NotInitialized , not a hidden start. Consequences ¶ One lifecycle contract per layer: construct, EnsureInitialized() , use, optionally Deinitialize() . Calling EnsureInitialized() before every use is cheap and safe, so code that is unsure whether the chip has started can call it; but the start-up cost is always paid at a call that says it starts something. Timing of a read is deterministic: it never includes a reset or a configuration write. Breaking for code written against ADR-0002: driver.Initialize(config) becomes Chip driver(port, config); then driver.EnsureInitialized() , and a restart with a new configuration becomes Deinitialize() , ApplyConfig() , EnsureInitialized() . The template and the first two migrated drivers (AS5047U, PCAL9555A) change with this ADR; the HardFOC drivers are migrated onto it. Alternatives considered ¶ Every read starts the chip on first use. Rejected: start-up traffic and start-up errors inside a read, and a failing chip retried at every read. Keep a public Initialize() for re-configuration. Rejected: ApplyConfig() already changes a running configuration, and a full restart is Deinitialize() then EnsureInitialized() , so a second entry point adds nothing but a way to restart by accident.
